situation.note: धंधे में बहुत घाटा हो गया है, कर्ज़ चढ़ गया है। बच्चों की फीस भरनी है। रात भर नींद नहीं आती, किसी से कह भी नहीं सकता।

understanding.bridge: What you are living with is what the texts call fear of what might happen, and that is where this week begins.

week_beats.hook: You recognise the sleeplessness and the debt as a fear that has a name.
week_beats.diagnose: You see that the sleeplessness is the fear of what it might mean, not the debt itself.
week_beats.steady: You hold that what is real in you cannot be taken by what has happened.
week_beats.act: You try doing one thing you can control today, and saying one true thing to one person.
week_beats.story: A man who lost everything shows you what standing again looks like from the inside.

understanding.core_struggle: His business has suffered heavy losses and debt has piled up; with children's fees due, he cannot sleep and cannot tell anyone.
understanding.mirror: You lie awake with the numbers and the children's fees, and you cannot bring yourself to say it out loud.
understanding.insight: The debt is real, but the sleeplessness is the fear of what it might mean for your children and your name. The two are not the same thing.

queries.hook: The weight of a failing business and mounting debt, with children's fees due, and the silence of not being able to tell anyone.
queries.diagnose: Fear grows from imagining the future and from forgetting that what is real in you cannot be lost; worry multiplies what has not happened.
queries.steady: What is real in you cannot be taken by what has happened; the effort you made is yours, and no result can take that away.
queries.act: Do your duty with the work you can control today, let the result go, and speak one true thing to one person you trust.
queries.story: A man who lost everything he built, facing his family and his own fear, yet finding the courage to stand again.

weeks: What remains when it is gone

verse.speaker: Arjuna
verse.setting: Krishna to Arjuna, who has collapsed in tears on the battlefield and refuses to fight.
verse.sanskrit: कार्पण्यदोषोपहतस्वभावःपृच्छामि त्वां धर्मसंमूढचेताः । यच्छ्रेयः स्यान्निश्चितं ब्रूहि तन्मेशिष्यस्तेऽहं शाधि मां त्वां प्रपन्नम् ॥
verse.line: I'm confused about what's right. Tell me plainly what's best; I'm ready to learn.
verse.translation: My nature is stricken by weakness and my mind is confused about what is right. I ask you: tell me for certain what is best for me. I am your student; I have come to you, teach me.
verse.why: Admitting you don't know and asking for help is where clarity begins.

matched.label: I can't handle not knowing what comes next

prasang.title: Krishna and Arjuna on Arjuna's faint-heartedness
prasang.summary: Krishna challenges Arjuna's despair. Arjuna admits he is confused about what is right, cannot tell which choice is better, and asks Krishna to teach him.
prasang.lesson: Admitting you don't know and asking for help is where clarity begins.

verse.meaning: Arjuna is on the battlefield. He has just seen his family and teachers standing on the other side. He is overwhelmed with grief and his body is shaking. He tells Krishna that his mind is confused about what is right and what is wrong. He admits that his nature is stricken by weakness. He asks Krishna to tell him plainly and for certain what is best. He says he is ready to learn and calls himself Krishna's student.
verse.for_you: You are sitting in the dark, and the debt is real. The sleeplessness is not just from the bills. It is the fear of what this means for your children and the name you have built. You do not know which way is right. You do not have to know.
verse.try_today: Write down one thing you are unsure about.
verse.scene_line: You stand in your own quiet room, asking for a clear path forward.
asks: How do I admit I am confused without shame?
Who can I ask for help without losing face?

verse.speaker: Janaka
verse.setting: Janaka, having chosen to keep ruling, talks gently to his own restless mind at night.
verse.sanskrit: यथा यथा विकल्पौघान्संकल्पयसि हेलया । तथा तथैति स्फारत्वं संसारस्तव चिन्तया ॥
verse.line: The more scenarios you spin, the bigger your world of worry grows.
verse.translation: The more you casually spin up fancies and possibilities, the more your world of troubles swells, through your own worrying.
verse.why: You don't have to leave your life to change it. Do the day's work with a mind that doesn't clutch.

matched.label: I can't sleep, my mind is racing
I feel anxious most of the time

prasang.title: King Janaka overhears the sages and keeps ruling, with a free mind
prasang.summary: Walking in his spring garden, King Janaka overhears hidden sages singing about the self. Shaken, he climbs to his palace roof and questions everything he has lived for. When his doorkeeper calls him to the day's work, he decides not to run away: he gets up and does his duties, but with a mind that no longer clutches.
prasang.story_hook: One spring morning, a king out for a walk overheard a song that he could not stop thinking about.
prasang.lesson: You don't have to leave your life to change it. Do the day's work with a mind that doesn't clutch.

verse.meaning: King Janaka sits on his palace roof, questioning the life he has built. His mind is a storm of what-ifs and futures that have not happened. He speaks to his own restless mind, telling it that every scenario it spins adds weight to a world that does not yet exist. The verse asks for a different kind of action. It asks to do the day's work without the mind clutching at the edges of what might go wrong.
verse.for_you: The sleeplessness is not the debt. It is the mind spinning futures for your children. The verse asks you to do the day's work with a mind that does not clutch at the edges of what might go wrong.
verse.try_today: Notice the moment the mind starts to spin futures and let the body rest in the room.
verse.scene_line: You are on your own roof, questioning the life you have built, while the doorkeeper waits.
asks: How do I stop the mind from spinning futures?
What does it mean to do my work without clutching?
Can I rest while the debt is still real?

verse.speaker: Bhartrihari
verse.sanskrit: पातितोऽपि कराघातैरुत्पतत्येव कन्दुकः । प्रायेण साधुवृत्तनामस्थायिन्यो विपत्तयः ॥
verse.line: A ball knocked down bounces back up. For good people, setbacks rarely last.
verse.translation: A ball struck down by the hand flies right back up. As a rule, the misfortunes of those who live rightly do not last.
verse.why: Setbacks rarely last for those who keep going on the right path.
verse.misuse: Not a promise that suffering is always short, or that people who suffer long did something wrong.

prasang.title: Nitishatakam: On steadfastness
prasang.summary: Steadfastness: the gods kept churning the ocean past jewels and poison until they found nectar; the steady do not leave the right path whatever people say. A struck ball bounces back and a cut tree grows again.
prasang.lesson: Setbacks rarely last for those who keep going on the right path.

verse.meaning: Bhartrihari speaks to the reader from the section on steadfastness. He says a ball knocked down by the hand flies right back up. He means setbacks rarely last for those who keep going on the right path.
verse.for_you: The losses are real, and the debt is real, but they do not have to be the last word on who you are. What you built and what you stand for is still there even when the numbers are not.
verse.try_today: Notice one small thing from your past that shows you kept going.
verse.scene_line: You are a ball on the ground, waiting for the next strike.
asks: How do I know if I am still on the right path?
What does it mean to keep going when the numbers are against me?
Can setbacks last even when I do everything right?

verse.speaker: Sugriva
verse.setting: Sugriva, who has lost his own wife and kingdom, steadies a grieving Ram.
verse.sanskrit: व्यसने वार्थकृच्छ्रे वा भये वा जीवितान्तगे। विमृशंश्च स्वया बुद्ध्या धृतिमान् नावसीदति॥
verse.line: In loss, money trouble or fear, the steady person thinks it through and does not go under.
verse.translation: In disaster, in money trouble, in fear, even when life itself is at stake, the steady person who thinks things through with their own mind does not sink.
verse.why: Two people in trouble can carry each other.

matched.label: I feel anxious most of the time

prasang.title: Ram and Sugriva's friendship
prasang.summary: Ram and Sugriva swear friendship before a fire. Sugriva shows Ram the jewels Sita dropped; Ram breaks down, and Sugriva comforts him: in trouble the steady person thinks it through, and a friend is the greatest refuge.
prasang.story_hook: Two exiles, each robbed of his wife and home, swore friendship over a fire.
prasang.lesson: Two people in trouble can carry each other.

verse.meaning: Sugriva speaks to Ram after Ram breaks down at the sight of Sita's jewels. Ram has lost Sita and his kingdom. Sugriva has lost his wife and his kingdom. Sugriva tells him that even when life itself is at stake, even in disaster and fear, a steady person thinks it through with their own mind and does not sink. The verse proposes that two people in trouble can carry each other, and that thinking through trouble with your own mind is how you stay afloat.
verse.for_you: You are carrying the debt and the sleepless nights, but your mind is the place where you can still stand. Think through the fear instead of letting it think for you. Your own mind is the steady ground.
verse.try_today: When the mind races tonight, name one fact and one fear.
verse.scene_line: You stand in the dark with the numbers, and the mind is your only refuge.
asks: How do I think through the fear without drowning in it?
What is one fact I can hold in my mind tonight?

verse.speaker: Vasishtha
verse.setting: The sage Vasishtha to Bharat, shattered by his father's death and Ram's exile.
verse.sanskrit: तात हृदयँ धीरजु धरहु करहु जो अवसर आजु। उठे भरत गुर बचन सुनि करन कहेउ सबु साजु ॥
verse.line: Keep courage in your heart, and do what today asks of you.
verse.translation: "Child, keep courage in your heart, and do what this moment asks of you today." Hearing his teacher, Bharat rose and had everything made ready.
verse.why: When head and heart disagree, go and face the person you think you wronged.

prasang.title: Bharat refuses the throne
prasang.summary: After the funeral, Vasishtha, the ministers and Kausalya all urge Bharat to rule, as his father wished. Bharat says the advice is right and his heart still isn't at peace; the crown means nothing without Ram. He decides to go to the forest, admit his fault, and trust his brother to forgive.
prasang.story_hook: Everyone agreed the throne was his, and Bharat could not bring himself to sit on it.
prasang.lesson: When head and heart disagree, go and face the person you think you wronged.

verse.meaning: Vasishtha speaks to Bharat, who is shattered by his father's death and his brother's exile. The king's ministers and mother urge Bharat to take the throne. Bharat agrees the advice is right, but his heart cannot find peace. He decides to go to the forest instead, admit his fault to Ram, and trust his brother to forgive. The verse tells him to keep courage in his heart and do what this moment asks of him.
verse.for_you: Your mind is full of what might happen, and your body is paying the price for it. You do not have to solve the whole night tonight.
verse.try_today: Do one thing you can control today, and say one true thing to one person.
verse.scene_line: You are at the edge of the forest, knowing the crown is not yours to wear.
asks: How do I find the courage to do what the moment asks?
What is the one true thing I should say to someone today?
How do I keep courage in my heart when everything feels lost?

verse.speaker: Teacher
verse.sanskrit: आचार्याय प्रियं धनमाहृत्य प्रजातन्तुं मा व्यवच्छेत्सीः । सत्यान्न प्रमदितव्यम् । धर्मान्न प्रमदितव्यम् । कुशलान्न प्रमदितव्यम् । भूत्यै न प्रमदितव्यम् । स्वाध्यायप्रवचनाभ्यां न प्रमदितव्यम् ॥
verse.line: Do not drift from truth or duty. Do not neglect your wellbeing, your prosperity, or your learning.
verse.translation: Having brought your teacher the gift he values, do not cut off the line of your family. Do not drift from truth. Do not drift from what is right. Do not neglect your wellbeing. Do not neglect your prosperity. Do not neglect study and teaching.
verse.why: Truth, right action, gratitude and graceful giving: a whole life in one speech.

matched.label: I'm burned out and running on empty

prasang.title: The graduation address
prasang.summary: As a student finishes his studies and leaves to start family life, the teacher gives him parting instructions: speak truth, do right, keep learning, honour mother, father, teacher and guest, give with grace. He even tells the student to copy only the teachers' good conduct, and when in doubt to act as thoughtful, gentle people would.
prasang.lesson: Truth, right action, gratitude and graceful giving: a whole life in one speech.

verse.meaning: The teacher speaks to a student who has completed his studies and is leaving the school. The moment is a graduation, a threshold. The teacher has just received a gift from the student and now gives a final charge. The student must not break the chain of family. The teacher tells them to stay close to truth and what is right. They must not let go of their own health, their ability to make a living, or their love of learning.
verse.for_you: Your business has lost money and the debt is heavy. That is real. Today, you can name that fear to someone you trust. It does not fix the debt.
verse.try_today: Tell one true thing to one person about what you are carrying.
verse.scene_line: You stand at the threshold of your own home, with the weight of your children's future in your hands.
asks: How do I tell my family the truth without breaking their trust?
What is the first true thing I can say out loud?
How do I keep my duty to my children while my own well-being fails?

story.title: Ram's grief and Lakshman's counsel
story.story_hook: He came back to the hut calling her name, and no one answered.
story.summary: Ram returns to an empty hut. He searches, questions trees and animals, breaks down and finally rages that he will destroy the world. Lakshman calms him: don't punish the whole world for one person's crime; trouble comes to everyone and passes.
story.lesson: In devastating loss, a steady friend can stop grief from turning into destruction.

anchor.speaker: Lakshman
anchor.setting: After Sita is taken, Ram in fury threatens to destroy the world; Lakshman steadies him.
anchor.sanskrit: एकस्य नापराधेन लोकान् हन्तुं त्वमर्हसि। ननु जानामि कस्यायं भग्नः सांग्रामिको रथः॥
anchor.line: Don't punish the whole world for one person's wrong.
anchor.translation: You should not destroy the worlds for the wrong done by one. Surely we can find out whose broken war chariot this is.
anchor.why: In devastating loss, a steady friend can stop grief from turning into destruction.

prasang.title: Ram's grief and Lakshman's counsel
prasang.summary: Ram returns to an empty hut. He searches, questions trees and animals, breaks down and finally rages that he will destroy the world. Lakshman calms him: don't punish the whole world for one person's crime; trouble comes to everyone and passes.
prasang.story_hook: He came back to the hut calling her name, and no one answered.
prasang.lesson: In devastating loss, a steady friend can stop grief from turning into destruction.

story.hook_title: Ram came back to the hut calling Sita's name, and no one answered
story.teaser: Ram came back to the hut calling Sita's name, and no one answered
story.for_you: Ram stood in an empty hut and wanted to burn the whole world down. You are in your own empty room, and the silence is loud. But the one who stays near you, your own steady hand, can stop the grief from eating the rest of your life.
asks: What is the one thing I can hold still this morning?
How do I stop the fear from destroying my peace?
Can I see this trouble as something that will pass?
